summary: Content splicing replaces part of a media stream with other content, such as an ad. The splicer needs to know when to start and end. This memo defines two RTP and RTCP extensions, so the splicing can be signaled.

plainLanguage.summary: It tells a TV system exactly when to switch from the show to a commercial and back again.

questions: what is the sdp splice group
subtitle: How a media sender tells a splicer exactly when to swap in other content, such as a regional ad.

tldr.problem: A splicer that swaps ads into an RTP stream needs to know when to start and end, but digging that timing out of the media payload is costly for a middlebox.
tldr.mechanism: The main sender puts a pair of NTP timestamps, the Splicing Interval, into an RTP header extension, and also sends the same pair in a new RTCP packet type (PT 213) in case the extension is stripped.
tldr.outcome: The splicer can switch between the main and substitutive streams at the right instants without inspecting payloads. SDP signaling uses a new SPLICE group semantic.

today: RFC 8286 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2017, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The Splicing Problem
sections.content:
Splicing replaces some multimedia content with other content for a period of time. In predictable cases such as advertisement insertion, the splice has to fit inside a designated time slot, so the splicer must first learn when to start and end. The RFC calls that information the Splicing Interval.

One existing method, [SCTE35], carries the Splicing Interval inside the MPEG2 transport stream layer in cable TV systems. When that stream is carried in RTP, a middlebox would have to decode RTP packets and search the payloads, which increases its workload and limits how many RTP sessions it can support.

This RFC instead defines an RTP header extension (RFC 8285) carrying the interval. Because a splicing-unaware middlebox might strip that extension, it also defines a new RTCP packet type as a complement, since RTCP is unreliable too and may not be as immediate.
sections.plainLanguage: Finding the commercial break time by opening up every video packet is slow. So the sender writes the times on the outside of the envelope instead.

sections.title: Splicers, Senders and the Splicing Interval
sections.content:
The main RTP sender authorizes a time window. The splicer receives both the main stream and the stream from a substitutive RTP sender but forwards only one at a time. A typical case is an IPTV provider replacing national ads with regional ones. The splicer can be an RTP mixer, which uses its own SSRC, sequence numbers and timing, or an RTP translator, which keeps the original SSRCs but must rewrite RTCP Sender Reports.

The Splicing Interval is a pair of NTP timestamps: the time of the first substitutive packet at the splicing-in point, and the time of the first main packet at the splicing-out point. The sender SHOULD send it more than once to mitigate loss, and MUST send it well in advance so the splicer can get the substitutive content before splicing starts.

The two senders MUST share a common reference clock, and the content providers MUST make sure the RTP timestamps of the first substitutive and first resumed main packets match the corresponding NTP timestamps.
sections.plainLanguage: There are two cameras and one person choosing which to show. The main camera says when to switch and when to switch back, and both cameras must use the same clock.

sections.title: The RTP Header Extension
sections.content:
The extension carries the splicing-out NTP timestamp in 7 octets (the lower 24 bits of the seconds field plus the 32-bit fraction), followed by the splicing-in timestamp as a full 64-bit NTP timestamp. The top 8 bits of the splicing-out value are inferred from the splicing-in value, assuming the out time is after the in time and the interval is less than 2^25 seconds. If the 7-octet out value is smaller than the in value's lower 7 octets, the top byte is the in value's top byte plus 0x01.

It can use either the one-byte or the two-byte header format of RFC 8285. Because extensions reduce RTP header compression efficiency, the sender is RECOMMENDED to include them in a number of packets before the splicing-in rather than all of them. The splicer, once it has the interval, is not allowed to include the extension in its own outgoing packets.
sections.plainLanguage: The note is a short stamp with two clock readings. To save space, the second reading leaves out its first digits, and the receiver works them out.

sections.title: The RTCP Splicing Notification Message
sections.content:
The main sender MUST also send the interval in a new RTCP packet type, whether or not it uses the header extension, and the two MUST be consistent. This is the safety net if a middlebox strips the extension. The message has version 2, a padding bit, packet type 213, a length, the SSRC of the main RTP sender, and the IN and OUT NTP timestamps as 64-bit values.

It can ride in a compound RTCP packet with the sender's Sender Report, or be sent as non-compound RTCP if that was negotiated (RFC 5506). If the RTP-to-NTP timestamp mapping changes, for example because of clock drift, an updated Sender Report or interval may be needed. The splicer is not allowed to forward this message to the receivers.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a backup copy of the note, sent through a different mailbox in case the first note gets thrown away on the way.

sections.title: Reducing Splicing Latency
sections.content:
When splicing starts or ends, receivers need certain Reference Information (the term comes from RFC 6285) before they can process the new content. Either the main or the substitutive sender SHOULD provide it together with its content. They also need synchronization metadata early enough, and the senders can estimate timing from the round-trip time as in RFC 3550.

If both senders provide the information, the splicer SHOULD pick one based on the situation, and adopting the mechanisms of RFC 6051 is RECOMMENDED to reduce synchronization delay.
sections.plainLanguage: When the show switches, viewers need a moment to catch up. Sending the catch-up information early keeps the picture from freezing.

sections.title: Failure Cases
sections.content:
A splicing-unaware middlebox may strip the extension, so the RFC describes a heuristic for the senders to check that the interval reached the splicer. The splicer may have its own SSRC and send reception reports, which lets senders spot problems on the path to it; or it may have no SSRC, which hides that. It can pass receiver reports back after modification, or withhold them. A splicer without its own SSRC has to forward and translate receiver reports, or senders will see no receivers. A mixer always has its own SSRC.

On detecting a failure, the splicer can use out-of-band signaling with the senders and fall back to payload-specific methods such as the MPEG2-TS splicing of [SCTE35], or simply abandon the splicing.
sections.plainLanguage: If the note might have been lost, the splicer can say so over another channel and use an old-fashioned way, or skip the commercial.

sections.title: SDP Signaling and IANA Registrations
sections.content:
The header extension is declared in an SDP extmap attribute with the URI urn:ietf:params:rtp-hdrext:splicing-interval. The RFC extends the SDP grouping framework (RFC 5888) with a new semantic, SPLICE, linking the main stream to the substitutive one. Only two m= lines are allowed in a SPLICE group, the main stream is the one with the extended extmap, and one m= line MUST NOT be in different SPLICE groups at once.

The RFC gives examples for declarative SDP, offer/answer without BUNDLE, and BUNDLE with all or only some media spliced. IANA registered the RTCP packet type SNM (Splicing Notification Message, value 213), the RTP compact header extension URI, and the SPLICE grouping semantic.
sections.plainLanguage: Before the show starts, the two sides agree which stream is the main one and which is the replacement, using a short setup message.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of RTP (RFC 3550), header extensions (RFC 8285) and the mixer and translator topologies apply. Splicing replaces content in RTP packets, so it breaks RTP-level end-to-end security such as source authentication and integrity protection. With SRTP the splicer would need the same security association as the main sender.

If the splicing times are confidential, the header extension MUST also be protected, for example with header extension encryption (RFC 6904). The splicer MUST have a way to authenticate the substitutive source, and authenticating the extension SHOULD be considered, since forged timing could make splicing fail or block receivers from the main content. A mixer that drops the CSRC list can allow loops, so non-RTP means MUST be used to detect and resolve them.
sections.plainLanguage: Swapping content means nobody can prove the video came straight from the original sender. The splicer must check that the replacement is real and the timing note is not faked.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Packet length in 32-bit words minus one.

fields.name: SSRC
fields.desc: SSRC of the main RTP sender.
